newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African women's investment firm Wiphold to list.
newsitem.headline: S.African women's investment firm Wiphold to list.

text.p: A South African investment firm that caters solely for women investors said on Tuesday it intends to list on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE).
Women Investment Portfolio Holdings Ltd (Wiphold) is currently launching a share offer only open to South African women, and says it aims for a public float eventually.
"Subject to unforeseen cirumstances, a listing of Wiphold will be sought in the foreseeable future," the firm said in its offer portfolio announcement.

Wiphold is currently offering shares at 200 cents each in a move that aims to raise between 20 and 40 million rand ($4.3 and $8.6 million) to help pay off some short-term debts, fund working costs and finance future projects.
Wiphold executive director Louisa Mojela told Reuters the offer would test the strength of the female-only market in South Africa for the first time.
"This will tell us how strong the market is. We are confident that the market is there, though it is currently an untapped market," she said.
Many women still occupy traditional roles in South African society, but Mojela said the day-to-day budgetting associated with running a home made them natural financial investors.
"They make investment decisions every day, just not in shares," she said.
Wiphold, with listed investments on the JSE worth 165.47 million rand at May 21, is still dwarfed by South Africa's major investment funds with billions of rands worth of assets.

But the firm is making an impact with significant holdings in Baobab Solid Growth Ltd, Bidvest Group Ltd and Smart Group Holdings Ltd. It also has minor holdings in Mustek Ltd and Carson Holdings Ltd.
The firm has also made some sharp investment moves, such as buying into Baobab at around 3.00 rand in 1995 and then watching the stock rocket up to its current level of 65.75 rand.
Mojela said Wiphold was the first and most established investment firm of its kind in South Africa and she added that she had not come across similar firms elsewhere in the world.
The company is open to women of all races, and was established because women are seen as one of the most disadvantaged groups in South Africa, she said.

Wiphold has encouraged other women-only groups to start setting up in South Africa and Mojela said she would like to see the concept take off elsewhere in Africa, especially to areas with developed investment sectors such as Kenya and Zimbabwe.
"We want to see this idea spreading out across the African continent," she said.
